claims.text: The eutectic high-entropy alloy contains distinct phases with different corrosion resistances.
The distinct phases have different mechanical properties.
Protective oxide layers form preferentially on the more corrosion-resistant phase.
Mechanical wear at elevated temperature disrupts the protective oxide layers.
Disruption of the oxide exposes a more chemically active, corrosion-sensitive phase.
The newly exposed active phase corrodes rapidly.
Localized corrosion weakens the local microstructure.
Corrosion-induced microstructural weakening increases susceptibility to subsequent mechanical wear.
Wear and corrosion therefore form a self-reinforcing degradation cycle.
At the relevant elevated temperature, oxide formation is promoted while oxide-layer stability is reduced.
The aggressive corrosive medium attacks the exposed corrosion-sensitive phase after oxide disruption.
Simultaneous wear and corrosion produce greater total material degradation than corrosion-only or wear-only exposure.
The combined condition increases the material-removal rate through increased wear.
The combined condition increases corrosion rates in regions where oxide protection is lost.
The proposed mechanism may not operate when the oxide layer is inherently robust.
The proposed mechanism may not operate when alloy modification produces more uniform phase-specific corrosion resistance.

contradictions.description: The predicted outcome invokes either corrosion-only or wear-only baselines, the baseline field alternatively proposes corrosion without wear or wear under a different oxide-stability temperature regime, and the actual experiment specifies only a corrosion-without-wear control. These are not equivalent matched baselines, so the stated comparison is internally inconsistent.
